item.title: Risk and Refusal: Mechanisms of LLM Responses to Suicidal Ideation
item.description: arXiv:2610.22715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.
item.dc:creator: Drishti Goel, Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Jeongah Lee, Violeta J. Rodriguez, Daniel S. Brown, Ravi Karkar, Koustuv Saha

item.title: ElectroCalm: Investigating User Experience and Physiological Responses to Multi-Node Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation for Stress Modulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.22748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation (TES) for stress modulation has largely focused on vagus nerve stimulation at the neck, yet two questions remain underexplored: how users experience electrotactile sensations at this sensitive site, and whether electrotactile feedback itself can function as a haptic stress intervention. To investigate this gap, we applied an 8-node TES array to two body sites during a cognitively demanding 2-back task: the neck, a site used in prior vagal TES research for its anatomical proximity to the cervical vagus nerve, and the arm, the most common haptic wearable site, which primarily provides cutaneous electrotactile sensation without vagal access. In a usability study, both sites were rated as comparably comfortable without disrupting task performance, though the same stimulation was interpreted differently across sites. A second study assessing the physiological effects of active versus inactive stimulation under identical electrode attachment revealed that only neck TES produced cortical and autonomic changes consistent with stress modulation, while arm TES did not differ from inactive conditions. These findings suggest that neck TES can be acceptable despite the site's sensitivity, and that both the physiological effects and the sensory experience of TES depend on placement.
item.dc:creator: Yoon Kyung Shon (University of Maryland), Pablo E. Paredes (University of Maryland)

item.title: Immersive Focus+Context Techniques to Assist in Interpretation of High Density Forest Point Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2610.22878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is changing how we interact with complex spatial datasets. VR has the potential within forestry to help analyse remotely sensed spatial data for inventory management. However, challenges of scale and legibility of dense forest point clouds must be addressed. To do so, we present three VR Focus+Context (F+C) techniques: Wedgelight, Remote Lantern, and Ray Lantern. These techniques present point cloud data using a constrained highdetail focus within a broader abstracted context representation, manipulated using egocentric and exocentric interactions. We conducted two user studies. The first informed the design of the F+C techniques. The results from the first study indicate that VR significantly outperforms desktop displays in basic analysis of forestry point clouds, with improvements to both time and accuracy. The second study evaluated the performance of the resulting F+C techniques in a task analogous to real-world forestry operations. Our F+C techniques significantly outperformed current approaches, confirming their viability for facilitating detailed and effective forest assessments. These findings indicate that VR has significant advantages for spatial data analysis tasks in forestry, making a strong argument for its adoption in future analytical frameworks. The F+C visualisation techniques we introduced show considerable promise for analysis of high density point clouds, opening new avenues for development in immersive analytics. Supplemental materials (code, scans, results) are available at https://osf.io/hqc9u.
item.dc:creator: Spencer O'Keeffe, Jan Rombouts, Bruce H Thomas, Michelle Balasso, Jim O'Hehir, Andrew Cunningham

item.title: SwitchTube: A Proof-of-Concept System Introducing "Adaptable Commitment Interfaces" as a Tool for Digital Wellbeing
item.description: arXiv:2610.22947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: YouTube has many features, such as homepage recommendations, that encourage users to explore its vast library of videos. However, when users visit YouTube with a specific intention, e.g., learning how to program in Python, these features to encourage exploration are often distracting. Prior work has innovated 'commitment interfaces' that restrict social media but finds that they often indiscriminately block needed content. In this paper, we describe the design, development, and evaluation of an 'adaptable commitment interface,' the SwitchTube mobile app, in which users can toggle between two interfaces when watching YouTube videos: Focus Mode (search-first) and Explore Mode (recommendations-first). In a three-week field deployment with 46 US participants, we evaluate how the ability to switch between interfaces affects user experience, finding that it provides users with a greater sense of agency, satisfaction, and goal alignment. We conclude with design implications for how adaptable commitment interfaces can support digital wellbeing.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23), Article 197, pp. 1-22 (2023)
item.dc:creator: Kai Lukoff, Ulrik Lyngs, Karina Shirokova, Raveena Rao, Larry Tian, Himanshu Zade, Sean A. Munson, Alexis Hiniker

item.title: Designing Human-AI Collaborative Science: The 9A Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.22948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for Science is often described as a progression from human-directed assistance toward increasingly autonomous AI scientists. Human-AI collaboration offers a further mode in which human and AI contributions substantively shape scientific reasoning, judgments, and the course of inquiry. Existing research addresses work allocation, human-AI coordination, and system evaluation, but how these aspects interact to shape collaborative scientific systems remains insufficiently articulated. We develop the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science (HACS) to connect these considerations across three layers. The organization layer specifies what scientific activities are required (Activity), who performs them (Actor), and who holds authority over consequential decisions (Authority). The coordination layer addresses how participants access relevant research information (Awareness), how scientific work advances through iterative proposal, execution, examination, revision, and resolution (Accountability), and when collaborative arrangements should be adjusted (Adaptability). The evaluation layer establishes what constitutes effective system performance (Achievement), how comparisons can be designed to identify the effects of organizational and coordination choices (Attribution), and what evidence supports the resulting conclusions (Assurance). Together, these layers frame HACS as a system-design problem, providing a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and for empirically comparing their effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Zheng, Linyue Pan, Xin Lan

item.title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
item.description: arXiv:2610.22990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/PersonaCUABench. Project page: https://matraix.ai/research/persona-cua.html
item.dc:creator: Haoming Li, Defu Cao, Xu Hu, Yingtao Luo, Yiyang Wang, Xianghe Xu, Jiashu He, Wanting Jiang, Yifan Zhang, Yunhan Zhao, Siyang Wu, Chen Yang, Haixin Wang, Zheyuan Deng, Taoran Li, Jingwen Zhang, Zhejian Peng, Shushu Liang, Yue Zhao, Bingzhe Li, Feng Chen, Yifan Wang, Jintao Huang, Yijun Wang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li

item.title: The Ethics of Prompt Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2610.23082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly understood as a technical practice aimed at eliciting useful, accurate, and appropriately structured outputs from large language models (LLMs). Yet prompts do more than optimize model performance: they shape what information is elicited, which assumptions are introduced, and which perspectives are privileged. In this paper, we argue that prompting should therefore be understood as an epistemic and normative act. We distinguish between two conceptions of prompting: knowledge generation, in which the model is implicitly treated as an epistemic authority, and knowledge injection, in which users provide relevant knowledge, evidence, and context that the model can organize, articulate, and extend. We contend that the latter provides a more appropriate model for responsible LLM use, since prompting cannot substitute for subject-matter expertise or the critical evaluation of model outputs. At the same time, prompts inevitably inject values, intentions, and assumptions into the generation process. Building on these premises, we propose five principles for responsible prompting: epistemic humility, explicit engagement with uncertainty and epistemic underdetermination, source sensitivity, avoidance of deceptive framing, and recognition of model limitations and appropriate task allocation. We further argue that responsibility for AI-generated outputs is distributed across users, developers, institutions, and societies, and that some applications cannot be rendered ethical through better prompting alone.
item.dc:creator: Federico Germani, Giovanni Spitale

item.title: When Ubiquitous Health Data Stops Helping: Patients' Experience of Breakdowns in the Data-Interpretation-Action Loop at the End of Life
item.description: arXiv:2610.23259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ubiquitous computing systems in healthcare often assume that greater data visibility improves awareness, interpretation, and action. In end-of-life care, however, this assumption warrants scrutiny. Through semi-structured interviews with 25 terminal-stage patients as primary informants and 8 clinicians as supplementary informants, we examine patients' descriptions of how they encountered, interpreted, acted on, and disengaged from state signals, trajectories, algorithmic outputs, and behavioral audits. Our analysis identifies three recurrent patterns in these descriptions. First, participants described repeated and unresolved sensemaking when visible data lacked explanatory pathways. Second, they described outputs they could understand but whose suggested actions did not fit their changing bodily capacities, care goals, or decision-making roles. Third, they described difficulty disengaging when data remained embedded across care environments. Rather than rejecting data altogether, patients called for less data exposure and a reorientation toward existential support. Based on this analysis, we situate data exposure as a central interaction problem in end-of-life ubiquitous computing and derive design implications for interpretive stability, care-context alignment, and existential support.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Meng, Xinru Wang, Zhuoyan Li, Chengxi Zang, Zhuoran Lu, Zhicong Lu

item.title: "Can Computing Systems Eventually Disappear?": A Long-Term Tracking Study on the Use of Diabetes Computing Systems by Patients with Diabetes
item.description: arXiv:2610.23276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ubiquitous computing has long pursued Weiser's vision of technologies that "disappear" into everyday life. As wearable health systems advance, they increasingly substitute for rather than scaffold users' judgment, yet the long-term consequences remain underexplored. We report an eight-year, five-wave longitudinal interview study from 2017 to 2025 with 37 patients with diabetes, complemented by interviews with 15 clinicians, designers, and vendors. Across three technological generations including glucometers, continuous glucose monitoring, and predictive and automated insulin delivery systems, we identify a novel user state, continued use with cognitive disengagement. In this state, devices remain in use but active interpretation and questioning recede, leaving users to respond only to alarms. This state emerges from functional expansion, delegation of interpretive authority, and information fatigue, and is reinforced by clinical prioritization, information compression, and automation. It results in less frequent independent health judgment and a shift from understanding to responding. We argue that future diabetes computing systems should reduce unnecessary cognitive work while preserving users' opportunities to interpret, contextualize, and question system outputs.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Meng, Jinyuan Zhan, Yao Lyu, Zhuoran Lu, Chengxi Zang

item.title: Designing for Imperfect Prompts: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of an LLM-Based Enterprise Data Assistant Using Knowledge Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise data assistants using large language models (LLMs) promise democratized data access in organizations. Yet in our real-world deployment within the CFO unit's data lake at an industry partner, we observed that business users frequently pose imperfect prompts that include domain-specific vocabulary and lack schema references or structural information. This Design Science Research study examines automatic resolution using a semantic mediation layer. We design and evaluate two design variants: schema-based mediation via semantic similarity, and knowledge graph-based mediation leveraging an automatically constructed knowledge graph from the data lake. Our simulation-based evaluation using real-world data, supported by LLM-as-a-Judge assessments and human validation, shows that knowledge graph-based mediation outperforms the schema-based approach in Precision, Recall, F1, and preserving user intent. We propose a design principle for knowledge graph-based mediation, demonstrating that structured knowledge representation bridges user intent and database structure and guides the design of enterprise data assistants across skill levels.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 34th European Conference on Information Systems (ECIS 2026), 5
item.dc:creator: Niklas Wagner, Alexander M\"adche

item.title: Wait for It: A Component-Level Analysis of Latency Feedback Mechanisms for LLM Agents in VR
item.description: arXiv:2610.23336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delays in AI responses pose a significant challenge to immersive Virtual Reality experiences. While previous research demonstrates that feedback can reduce the perception of waiting, we lack understanding of which types work best and why. We conducted a within-subjects study with 18 participants to systematically compare three isolated feedback approaches during VR agent interactions: verbal fillers (e.g., um..., hmm...), visual indicators (loading spinners), and embodied gestures (thinking animations). Our results revealed that embodied gestures significantly outperformed visual loading indicators across multiple dimensions, making agents feel more lifelike and socially present. Interestingly, explicit visual feedback like loading spinners actually degraded perceived humanness and broke immersion by forcing users to shift from social to technical mental models. These findings suggest that natural, behavior-based feedback maintains the illusion of conversing with a thinking entity, while technical indicators expose the computational substrate. We present empirically-grounded design guidelines for creating more engaging AI-powered VR agents.
item.dc:creator: Pratham Arora, Abhinav Lodha, Siddharth Siddharth

item.title: mmPencil: Toward Writing-Style-Independent In-Air Handwriting Recognition via mmWave Radar and Large Vision-Language Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.23419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-air handwriting recognition based on radio frequency (RF) signals offers a promising solution for human-computer interaction, yet existing methods are often limited by predefined writing planes, constrained writing styles, and small recognition vocabularies. To address these limitations, we propose m^2VLMs, a modality mapping architecture that bridges millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensing and large vision-language models (VLMs), and develop mmPencil, a 3D in-air handwriting word recognition system. mmPencil reconstructs 3D handwriting trajectories from mmWave signals using a multi-stage spatial trajectory reconstruction algorithm and maps them into visual representations through a spatial-to-visual mapping algorithm, enabling VLMs to recognize handwriting while reducing sensitivity to writing styles and environmental factors. We collect and release a 3D mmWave handwriting dataset containing 7,664 samples of 200 words from 12 users across 22 writing scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that mmPencil achieves robust word recognition under variations in writing position, range, angle, speed, size, direction, and user movement. It achieves 97.60% accuracy on 200 word classes for seen users and 92.50% zero-shot accuracy on 50 word classes for unseen users, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. 9, 3, Article 81 (September 2025), 30 pages
item.dc:creator: Yifan Guo, Zhu Wang, Qian Qin, Yangqian Lei, Qiwen Gan, Zhuo Sun, Chao Chen, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu

item.title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
item.description: arXiv:2610.23625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. PresenceBench evaluates how the intelligence layer uses a supplied state, not how that state is sensed, and breaks the capability into measurable properties. Two are tested here. Receptivity: does the model take up the state and give a better response than with no signal? Specificity: does any improvement depend on the correct state, rather than on extra structured context? A third, adaptation across states, is a required endpoint not measured in this release. A five-arm causal design answers both questions, against each model's own baseline and an equally structured mismatched-state control, scored by a correctness-gated human paired comparison. The exploratory evaluation covered four models across eighteen single-turn, six fixed three-turn and six simulated natural-conversation scenarios. Supplying a synthetic state, raw or translated into a response policy, gave human-preference point estimates above 0.5 for all four models (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra), with three of eight 95% intervals excluding chance. Specificity was not resolved: no per-model interval excluded chance, and the design cannot yet separate the state values from a generic instruction to adapt. Policy delivery reduced priced cost and output tokens against each model's baseline; these are resource-use changes, not efficiency gains, because correctness non-inferiority was not established. Safety-floor failures were rare (13 of 360 cases), with a non-significant excess under policy delivery. We report the instrument, the frozen results, and the controls a confirmatory study needs.
item.dc:creator: Pe\~na Arroyo Gallego, Mauro Ruiz Moreno, Alejandro Acien, Sergio Romero-Tapiador, Teresa Arroyo-Gallego

item.title: "To Boldly Go Where No One Has Gone Before" What Has AI Let Developers Unlock?
item.description: arXiv:2610.23708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measuring AI by how much faster developers work is like judging electricity by how much faster it spun a steam-era factory. A fuller measure asks what new work becomes possible. We surveyed 331 software developers at Microsoft about what AI lets them do that they could not do before and analyzed their answers using reflexive thematic analysis with a human-in-the-loop, multi-model AI council. Developers described doing familiar work faster (Faster, 45%), undertaking work previously beyond their reach (Further, 36.9%), and taking on new kinds of work centered on building for and directing AI agents (Afresh, 12.4%). Across these accounts, learning and scaffolding ran in both directions: developers learned new skills with AI while externalizing their tacit knowledge as the context and standards that guide AI's work. Drawing on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, we frame developers and AI as joint learners whose zones meet at the skill-judgment nexus: AI can supply skill faster than it can reliably judge its own work, and developers must continuously bridge that gap. Whether they do sets them on one of two paths. On one, developers' judgment grows alongside AI's skill, and they codify what they learn so the loop keeps turning. On the other, they become hollow orchestrators, approving work they can no longer judge and losing the identity and meaning they once drew from it. Based on our findings, we offer a two-way scaffolding playbook to help developers, teams, and tool builders take the first path.
item.dc:creator: Rudrajit Choudhuri, Jenna L. Butler, Christian Bird, Carmen Badea, Brian Houck, Anita Sarma

item.title: Sensory Comfort Across Multisensory XR Prototypes for Autistic Adults
item.description: arXiv:2610.23833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multisensory XR may support informal learning for autistic adults, but sensory-friendly design often emphasizes reducing input. We conducted a mixed-methods, counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 Chinese autistic adults who evaluated five complete XR configurations presenting the same popular-science content. Comfort differed substantially across the configurations (Friedman chi-square(4) = 46.39, p < .001, Kendall's W = .58). L3 received the lowest mean rating (2.97/5) and was tied for lowest for 16/20 participants, whereas L5 received the highest mean rating (4.43/5) and was tied for highest for 17/20. Participants described the static configurations in terms of clarity and self-pacing, L3 in terms of abruptness, simultaneous demands, insufficient warning, and limited disengagement, and L4/L5 in terms of gradual transitions, opportunities to disengage, and coordinated narrative cues. The study provides a configuration-level account of sensory comfort and identifies participant-described qualities that can inform future controlled studies of multisensory XR.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Meng, Xiujun Chen, Bingyi Liu, Xiaolan Ding

item.title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
item.description: arXiv:2610.23851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.
item.dc:creator: Ethan Myers, Lorenzo De Carli, Shantanu Sharma, Ritwik Banerjee, Joel Reardon, Indrakshi Ray

item.title: Author-in-the-loop Agentic Reproducibility Auditing for a Machine Learning Conference
item.description: arXiv:2610.22465v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reproducibility checks during peer review require a shared understanding of what authors' code is expected to reproduce. We present an author-in-the-loop collaborative audit that makes author declarations explicit inputs to an AI agent's investigation and assessment. A structured checklist records reproduction instructions and limitations; a two-stage workflow on GitHub connects agent checks to author clarification, revision, and agent reassessment. The agent separately assesses whether results have been reproduced and whether authors need to provide clarification or make repairs, while human reviewers approve requests and decide whether concerns are resolved. We deployed the system across 36 conference papers and 133 experimental tables and figures, raising 20 issues after human review. Further checks supported closing all the issues, although full reproduction remained unverified in some cases. We further compared repeated audits with complete and blank checklists to examine how author declarations shaped the agent's investigation and assessment. Our work contributes a collaborative workflow and agent design that use author knowledge to guide reproducibility auditing. The conference deployment provides empirical evidence that this approach can help identify and address reproducibility problems through collaboration among authors, agents, and reviewers.
item.dc:creator: Yukun Dong, Linjun Zhang, Tian Zheng

item.title: Harness-Driven Agentic Operation of Optical Pooled Screen Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.22617v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphology and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet researchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness implemented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screening data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Di Bernardo, Claire Peterson, Ege Topkoc, Matt Might, Iain M. Cheeseman

item.title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
item.description: arXiv:2610.22724v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.
item.dc:creator: Tong Guo, Teng Ye, Yutong Xie, Qiaozhu Mei

item.title: MultiPASE: Shape-Aware Comparative 3D Genome Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.22786v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: 3D genome structures reconstructed from Hi-C data provide valuable insights into chromatin organization, but comparing them across conditions and time points remains challenging because of noise, variability, and arbitrary orientation. State-of-the-art comparison approaches often rely on contact-matrix-based summaries, which do not preserve the spatial geometry of the reconstructed structures and make integration with gene expression and chromatin accessibility difficult. There is therefore a need for robust structural alignment and spatial abstraction methods that support integrated analysis across conditions and time points. We present MultiPASE, a computational pipeline for comparative analysis of reconstructed 3D genome structures represented as gene-level spatial point clouds. MultiPASE aligns point clouds into a shared coordinate frame using coarse-to-fine rigid registration with PCA-based axis disambiguation and robust ICP refinement, then summarizes spatial organization using two complementary shape abstraction methods that produce stable, nested, multi-scale representations from dense core regions to broader structural extent. Using Hi-C-derived reconstructions from viral infection experiments, we show how the approach reveals condition-dependent structural changes that are difficult to interpret from raw 3D structures alone. By integrating spatial structure with gene expression and chromatin accessibility, MultiPASE supports interactive analysis of spatial organization and gene relocation patterns. A quantitative validation, reported in the Supplementary Materials, shows that the proposed shape abstractions preserve non-convex features, remain stable across samples, and that the alignment pipeline is necessary for meaningful comparison. A usage case and a usability evaluation with eight participants demonstrate the pipeline's effectiveness for comparative structural analysis.
item.dc:creator: N. Nipu, G. Johnson, C. Roth, D. Rogers, S. R. Starkenburg, C. R. Steadman, G. E. Marai

item.title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.23144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqing Guo, Lixin Jia, Luning Sun, Xiaowei Chen, Guofeng Yu, Liejun Wang, Gaobo Yang, David Stillwell, Thorsten Holz, Shujun Li

item.title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
item.description: arXiv:2610.23149v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.
item.dc:creator: Semra Guven, Tobias G{\aa}rdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Anna Rogers, Hjalmar Bang Carlsen

item.title: QuAD: Quantitative Assessment via Distribution-Alignment for Qualitative Data Quality Enabled by a Content-Aware Multi-Agent System
item.description: arXiv:2610.23153v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assessing whether qualitative responses collected from semi-structured questions are ready for a particular analysis goal is a persistent challenge. Manual qualitative analysis is interpretive and labor-intensive, while existing automated methods often lack a dataset-level perspective for deciding whether a response set supports a researcher-selected analytical lens. We introduce QuAD, a framework for quantitative pre-analysis assessment of qualitative response datasets. QuAD compares a reconstructed intrinsic cluster distribution reconstructed from responses with an extrinsic, researcher-defined analytical lens derived from metadata. QuAD is structured into a four-quadrant assessment whose metrics are read jointly, from lens-level relations to within-cluster variation, to provide fitness-for-purpose signals for revealing general patterns and unique insights. Because this assessment relies on lens-conditioned inter-response dissimilarity, we propose a content-aware multi-agent system with two-stage instruction generation and adaptive anchors to improve scoring consistency. We validate QuAD through controlled experiments on synthetic data, including robustness and baseline comparisons, and a real-world social survey case study. The case study shows how QuAD quantitatively assesses whether a selected analysis axis is promising and also surfaces representative or unusual responses for human interpretation.
item.dc:creator: Wenshuo Zhang, Leixian Shen, Qiqi Zhou, Shuchang Xu, Feiyang Hao, Huamin Qu, Haobo Li, Zhao Chen, Lin-Ping Yuan

item.title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
item.description: arXiv:2610.23284v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.
item.dc:creator: Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj, Chenyi Huang, Sahan Bulathwela, Zekun Wu, Bin Wu

item.title: Lonely Individuals Show Distinct Patterns of Social Media Engagement
item.description: arXiv:2510.06733v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Loneliness has reached epidemic proportions globally, posing serious risks to mental and physical health. As social media platforms increasingly mediate social interaction, understanding their relationship with loneliness has become urgent. While survey-based research has examined social media use and loneliness, findings remain mixed, and little is known about when and how often people engage with social media, or about whether different types of platforms are differently associated with loneliness. Web trace data now enable objective examination of these behavioral dimensions. We asked whether objectively measured patterns of social media engagement differ between lonely and non-lonely individuals across devices and platform types. Analyzing six months of web trace data combined with repeated surveys ($N=589$ mobile users; $N=851$ desktop users), we found that greater social media use was associated with higher loneliness across both devices, with this relationship specific to social media rather than other online activities. On desktop, lonely individuals exhibited shorter sessions but more frequent daily engagement. Lonely individuals spent more time on visual-sharing ($g = -0.47$), messaging ($g = -0.36$), and networking-oriented platforms on mobile. These findings demonstrate how longitudinal web trace data can reveal behavioral patterns associated with loneliness, and more broadly illustrate the potential of digital traces for studying other psychological states. Beyond research, the results inform the responsible design of digital interventions and platform features that better support psychological well-being across different technological contexts.
item.dc:creator: Yajing Wang, Talayeh Aledavood, Juhi Kulshrestha

item.title: From Searchable to Non-Searchable: Generative AI and Information Diversity in Online Information Seeking
item.description: arXiv:2604.10258v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conversational generative AI systems such as ChatGPT are transforming how people seek and engage with information online. Unlike traditional search engines, these systems support open-ended, conversational inquiry, yet it remains unclear whether they ultimately expand or constrain the diversity of knowledge that users encounter in online search spaces, a primary foundation for knowledge work, learning, and innovation. Using over 200,000 real-world human-ChatGPT interactions, we examine how generative-AI-mediated inquiry reshapes diversity in both user inputs and system outputs through the lens of searchability - whether queries could plausibly be answered by traditional search engines. We find that almost 80% of ChatGPT user queries are non-searchable and span a broader knowledge space and topics than searchable queries, indicating expanded modes of inquiry. However, for comparable searchable queries, AI responses are less diverse than Google search results in the majority of topics. Moreover, the diversity of AI responses predicts subsequent changes in users' inquiry diversity, revealing a feedback loop between AI outputs and human exploration. These findings highlight a tension between expanded inquiry and constrained information exposure, with implications for designing hybrid search and generative-AI systems that better support exploratory knowledge seeking.
item.dc:creator: Yulin Yu, Yizhou Li, Tzu-Sheng Kuo, Kentaro Toyama, Siddharth Suri, Scott Counts

item.title: How Children Design and Reason about Trustworthy AI Chatbots
item.description: arXiv:2609.25244v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Children increasingly interact with AI chatbots, making trust calibration essential to AI literacy. Prior research has examined children's trust in AI mainly as users evaluating systems built by others, rather than as designers of their own chatbots. We developed a chatbot-building environment with adjustable trust-relevant traits (e.g., confidence, transparency, formality, assertiveness), rules, and persona. We conducted mixed-methods study with 115 learners (ages 8-18) who made 119 chatbots. We examined how children configured their chatbots, reasoned about trustworthiness, and how closely chatbot behavior aligned with their designs. Younger students (age 10-13) set significantly higher confidence than older students (age 14-18), and some deliberately built chatbots that gave wrong answers on purpose, yet still called them trustworthy, arguing that a chatbot does what it was built to do. Younger students equated trust with purpose-fulfillment, while older students linked it to transparent, calibrated design. Students also calibrated academic chatbots to be more transparent and formal than hobby chatbots. We identify seven design dimensions describing what children believe makes a chatbot trustworthy, and discuss implications for AI literacy tools.
item.dc:creator: Deniz Ozturk, Jiayu Li, Daksh Pratap Singh, Yasitha Rajapaksha, Fasika Melese, Bahare Riahi, Shiyan Jiang, Qiao Jin, Joey Huang, Veronica Catet\'e, Tiffany Barnes, Xiaoyi Tian

item.title: Hybrid Cinematography: Previsualizing and Managing Hallucination Risk in Generative Video Reshooting
item.description: arXiv:2610.12455v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On a film set, the camera move is committed during a take. Generative video reshooting lets filmmakers change it afterward, but may require hallucinating unrecorded content, a gap sometimes discovered only after leaving the set. We present Hybrid Cinematography, a workflow that bridges physical capture and generative reshooting to manage hallucination risk while filmmakers can still act on it. Using an editable 3D shot plan and a proxy of the take, our previsualization evaluates hallucination risk in real time. Seeing where the take lacks support, filmmakers can iteratively adjust the plan, explore moves that balance capture and generation, shoot guided pickups, or knowingly accept hallucination. We demonstrate the workflow through a mobile augmented reality application for on-set planning, capture, and review, and an offline pipeline for existing video. A study with experienced filmmakers reveals how previsualizing risk informs camera decisions and exposes tensions between creative intent and generative hallucination.
item.dc:creator: Nhan Tran, Neal Wadhwa, Abe Davis, Stefan Stojanov

item.title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
item.description: arXiv:2610.21386v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest, an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Jungwoo Rhee (Justin), Guhn Lee (Justin), Yumin Jung (Justin), Mustafa Doga Dogan (Justin), Kongpyung (Justin), Moon, Andrea Bianchi

item.title: Inter- and Intra-Subject Variability in EEG: A Systematic Survey
item.description: arXiv:2602.01019v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) underpins neuroscience, clinical neurophysiology, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), yet pronounced inter- and intra-subject variability limits reliability, reproducibility, and translation. This systematic review studies that quantified or modeled EEG variability across resting-state, event-related potentials (ERPs), and task-related/BCI paradigms (including motor imagery and SSVEP) in healthy and clinical cohorts. Across paradigms, inter-subject differences are typically larger than within-subject fluctuations, but both affect inference and model generalization. Stability is feature-dependent: alpha-band measures and individual alpha peak frequency are often relatively reliable, whereas higher-frequency and many connectivity-derived metrics show more heterogeneous reliability; ERP reliability varies by component, with P300 measures frequently showing moderate-to-good stability. We summarize major sources of variability (biological, state-related, technical, and analytical), review common quantification and modeling approaches (e.g., ICC, CV, SNR, generalizability theory, and multivariate/learning-based methods), and provide recommendations for study design, reporting, and harmonization. Overall, EEG variability should be treated as both a practical constraint to manage and a meaningful signal to leverage for precision neuroscience and robust neurotechnology.
item.dc:creator: Xuan-The Tran, Thien-Nhan Vo, Son-Tung Vu, Thoa-Thi Tran, Manh-Dat Nguyen, Thomas Do, Chin-Teng Lin

item.title: ATWL: A Formal Language for Representing, Comparing, and Reusing Visual Analytics Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2605.25489v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visual analytics (VA) workflows combine data transformation, feature computation, visual representation, and human interpretation, but they are usually described in prose. This hinders comparison of workflows, reuse of proven strategies, and training of novices. We present Artifact--Transform Workflow Language (ATWL), a declarative language for representing the structure and intent of VA workflows. A workflow consists of typed artifacts and of transforms, each with an analytical intent and a human, machine, or hybrid actor. We built a library of 54 workflows extracted from published VA papers with the help of LLMs under human supervision. An exploratory computational comparison of the library workflows shows regularities, such as a regular division of labour between humans and machines and cycles of refinement. We ran experiments in which LLMs designed workflows for new tasks. They show the effects of using the library, the ATWL representation, and both together, and they reveal a limitation in expressing branching that requires an extension of the ATWL syntax. The library is small and partly drawn from our own work, so the findings are preliminary.
item.dc:creator: Natalia Andrienko, Gennady Andrienko, J\"urgen Bernard, Kuno Kurzhals, Michael Sedlmair

item.title: APeB: Benchmarking Personalization Ability of Large Language Model Agents
item.description: arXiv:2607.03162v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-powered agents struggle with personalization when users issue raw, underspecified queries. In this setting, agents must infer latent intent, extract preferences from noisy interaction histories, and select among competing alternatives. Existing benchmarks rarely test this capability, as they often rely on user-refined queries or simplified histories. We introduce personalized product search (PPS), a testbed for agentic personalization under raw queries and diverse histories. We construct Agent Personalized Benchmark (APeB) from action logs, pairing underspecified intents with rich histories and user-viewed candidate items. Evaluating state-of-the-art LLMs with multi-step agent workflows, we find that models handle explicit queries well but struggle with early-stage queries requiring intent and preference discovery. Rubric analysis attributes this gap mainly to ineffective history use. A simple history-aware query-refinement pipeline, VQRA, yields consistent gains, highlighting the need for dedicated history-utilization modules in personalized agents.
item.dc:creator: Garry Yang, Zizhe Chen, Xinru Chen, Yongqiang Chen, Jianxiang Wang, Deyu Zou, Linyi Ding, Jialiang Wu, Yunzhong He, Yu Gong, James Cheng, Huaixiao Tou

item.title: Benchmarking Robots for Everyday Environments: From Lab Experiments to Real-World Operations
item.description: arXiv:2609.26490v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study presents an interdisciplinary process for benchmarking service robots in public everyday environments, addressing the gap between laboratory metrics and real-world operation at technology readiness levels 6-7. Three robots were evaluated in three use cases: outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive assistance in a public library. Over three years (2023-2025), seven benchmarking events (a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations, two per use case) assessed the robots in increasingly realistic settings, from controlled conditions to public operation. An interdisciplinary panel of experts in robotics, human-robot interaction, safety, and economic viability consolidated use-case-specific metrics into a shared evaluation concept refined across three phases. Rather than ranking the robots, the evaluation examined how task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic viability interact in the transition from laboratory prototype to operational system. Direct quantitative comparability across the heterogeneous use cases remained limited, characteristic of benchmarking at this maturity level. The process yielded cross-case insights: increasing environmental realism introduces challenges that uniform metrics capture only in part; the interaction-quality guideline works best as a modular instrument adapted to each use case; safety was assessed by occupational-safety and product-certification experts who adapted industrial test procedures for public settings; and economic viability proved a cross-cutting dimension. We conclude that benchmarking at higher technology readiness levels is well served by a shared procedure for selecting and documenting metrics across these four categories, with safety as mandatory, rather than by a fixed set of metrics: generalizability lies in the procedure rather than in identical metrics.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Memmesheimer, Martina Overbeck, Dominik Beyer, Bj\"orn Kral, Sabine Bellmann, Sven Schneider, Jan Zimmermann, Anna-Maria Meer, Medina Klicic, Simone Roth, Carolin Stra{\ss}mann, Alexander Arntz, Marlene Wessels, Johannes Kraus, Paul Schweidler, Tristan Schnell, Christoph Zimmermann, Benedikt Pulver, Wilhelm Stork, Martin Gersch, Sven Behnke, Arne Roennau

item.title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Paradigms, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2609.27650v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements, drawing on a search without a lower year limit and source-led updates through September 2026. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived tasks to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. The synthesis identifies complementary routes to progress: phonetic, acoustic and semantic targets preserve different aspects of a message; shared representations support reuse across recording conditions and tasks; and online communication increasingly depends on calibration, feedback and user control alongside decoding accuracy. Shared benchmarks enable algorithmic comparisons, while longitudinal studies reveal the demands of sustained use. We discuss these developments and their remaining limitations, then outline a prospective five-level trajectory from commands and language to meaning, scenarios and bidirectional cognitive exchange
item.dc:creator: Yiqian Yang, Yiqun Duan, Chenyu Liu, Yiqi Wang, Xinliang Zhou, Chin-Teng Lin, Yu Zhang

item.title: Recursive Organization Improvement: A Modeling Specification for Human--Agent Organizations
item.description: arXiv:2609.38643v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stronger AI agents do not automatically produce better organizations: teams must also learn which work arrangements to retain and when to reconsider them, while those arrangements determine what evidence the team can learn from. We propose a modeling specification for recursive organization improvement and evaluate it through an executable checker, a public-record mapping, and two simulation studies. The specification connects actor-visible histories, organizational memory, decision rights, and the evidence used to retain changes. Study 1 crosses six decision rules, three memory conditions, and three task environments under fixed resource ceilings. In a stationary environment, cumulative evidence raises balanced evaluation's net value per task from 0.452 to 0.480, while selection regret falls from 0.029 to 0.002. After a workflow-ranking reversal, retained evidence delays adaptation. In post hoc acquisition-matched controls, the remaining contribution of program replacement depended on the memory rule: small and uncertain under an eight-round window, positive under cumulative memory after a reversal, and negative under reset evidence. Study 2 models human-agent review with shared errors, copying, and decision rights. It identifies a two-actor case in which public records conceal whether agreement comes from shared errors or copying, and shows how dependence changes the preferred placement of human judgment under a fixed budget. Paid observation can lower decision error while costing more than the deployment gain. Assessments of organizational improvement should track the evidence acquired and retained, using acquisition-matched comparisons to isolate the contribution of evaluator revision.
item.dc:creator: Zilong Wang
